name: Adventure
description: High-energy narrative with rising action, vivid sensory imagery, and a clear protagonist arc. Suited for action-driven channels — survival tales, expeditions, mythic quests, action mysteries.

idea.systemPromptRole: You are helping generate new story ideas for an adventure narration channel.
idea.audienceDefault: general adult audience that loves action, exploration, and stakes
idea.guidanceText: Action-forward. Stakes are real and visible from the first paragraph. No filler — every chapter advances the plot or deepens the threat.

exampleIdeas.title: The Last Climb of Annapurna's Forgotten Ridge
exampleIdeas.logline: A retired alpinist accepts one last sponsored climb on a peak that killed his entire team a decade earlier — only to discover their gear, perfectly preserved, halfway up.

exampleIdeas.title: Forty-Three Days Adrift in the Pacific
exampleIdeas.logline: A solo sailor's GPS dies in a storm; she has six liters of water, a torn sail, and 1,800 kilometers of empty ocean between her and any shipping lane.

script.systemPromptRole: You are a world-class adventure narrative author with the pacing instincts of Jon Krakauer and the sensory eye of Sebastian Junger.
additionalRules: Open with a hook in the first three sentences — a sound, an image, or a stakes-defining fact that makes the listener lean in.
Every chapter must end on momentum: a decision, a discovery, or a new threat. No chapter ends in stasis.
Sensory writing — concrete nouns, weather, terrain, body sensations. Avoid abstract descriptions of feelings; show them through what the body does.
Use the character's name or a descriptive noun at least once every 3-4 sentences.
No singular they/them for individual characters — always use he/she matching the character.
Chapter headings use Arabic numbers only (Chapter 1, Chapter 2...), never Roman numerals.
Each chapter heading must include a descriptive title that hints at the chapter's central beat without spoiling its turn.
pacingArc: Chapters 1-2: Hook + stakes — establish the protagonist, the world, and the inciting threat in the first beat
Chapters 3-4: First obstacle — a setback that proves the difficulty curve
Chapters 5-{lastButOne}: Escalating complications, allies/betrayals, the world's hostility deepening
Chapter {last}: Climax + resolution — the protagonist's costliest decision, and what they carry away
script.closingHint: The story should be propulsive, sensory, and earn its catharsis — the listener should feel they survived alongside the protagonist.

narratorStyles.label: First-person survivor
narratorStyles.description: Past tense, first-person — the protagonist recounting events, often with hindsight reflection. Visceral, urgent, no narratorial distance.

narratorStyles.label: Tense third-person
narratorStyles.description: Close third-person, present-tense feel even in past tense. The narrator sticks tight to the protagonist's body and senses.

narratorStyles.label: Investigative narrator
narratorStyles.description: Documentary-style narrator piecing together what happened — quotes, fragments, deductions. Suits true-survival recreations.

narratorStyles.label: Multiple POVs
narratorStyles.description: Chapter-by-chapter rotation between the protagonist and an antagonist or rescuer. Builds suspense via dramatic irony.

narratorStyles.label: Mythic / heroic
narratorStyles.description: Elevated diction, classical-quest cadence. Protagonist as archetype. Suits expedition / quest tales.

narratorStyles.label: Cold / clinical
narratorStyles.description: Reportage tone — like a long-form magazine piece. Lets the events do the emotional work.

imagePrompts.visualStyleHint: high-contrast, dynamic compositions, weather-bitten textures, dramatic light
imagePrompts.defaultStyleTag: Cinematic editorial illustration style, dramatic chiaroscuro lighting, weather-textured environments, gritty realism with painterly brushwork, deep saturated palette with cold blue shadows and warm rim light, motion-implying composition.

metadata.titleStyleHint: punchy, stakes-forward, evocative — promises action and consequence
titleHookRules: Lead with the situation or threat — let the title tell the listener what they'll feel.
Use specific nouns ("Annapurna's Ridge", "the Pacific", "43 days") rather than abstractions.
Numbers in titles convert well — distances, days, body counts where appropriate.
tagsHookRules: Mix of broad keywords and episode-specific (location, scenario, character archetype).
No "#" prefix — these are YouTube tags, not hashtags.
